interviewQuestions.question: What problem does a semantic or metrics layer actually solve, and why can't dashboards just agree on definitions informally?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It solves definitional drift — the fact that "active user" or "revenue" sounds unambiguous but every team that builds a dashboard makes an independent judgment call about time windows, exclusions, and edge cases. Five reasonable choices produce five slightly different numbers, and when two dashboards get compared side by side, it looks like a data quality failure when the data itself was never wrong.

Informal agreement doesn't hold at scale because there's no enforcement mechanism — a shared wiki page saying "active means logged in in 7 days" doesn't stop someone from writing their own SQL that's close but not identical, especially under deadline pressure with no easy way to discover the official definition first.

A metrics layer fixes this structurally: each metric is defined once, in version-controlled code, and every consumer — BI tool, notebook, ad-hoc query — resolves the metric by name against that single definition instead of deriving their own. Changing the definition is a one-line, reviewed pull request that updates the number everywhere it's used, instead of a wiki edit nobody re-reads.

**Testing:** whether you understand this as a governance/enforcement problem, not a communication problem that a shared doc could solve.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How would you design the primitives of a metric definition — what does a well-specified metric actually need to capture?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd build it from three primitives that map onto ordinary dimensional-modeling vocabulary: a **measure** (the underlying additive quantity, like a count or a sum of a fact column), a **grain** (the level it's computed at, like per user per day), and the **dimensions** it can legitimately be sliced by (region, plan tier, cohort).

Concretely, `active_users` would be: measure = `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)`, filter = `last_active_at >= now() - 7 days AND is_bot = false`, grain = daily, slicing dimensions = region, plan_tier, signup_cohort. Every one of those choices — the 7-day window, excluding bots — is a real decision that used to live differently in five people's heads; writing it down as a single reviewed artifact is the whole point.

I'd also insist on a name, an owner, and a description as first-class fields, not just the SQL logic — when someone questions why a number looks off, "who owns this and what's the intended definition" needs to be answerable in seconds, not by reverse-engineering a query.

**Testing:** whether you can decompose a fuzzy business term into the concrete, reviewable pieces a metrics layer actually needs.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design

interviewQuestions.question: You're asked to roll out a metrics layer at a company where 40+ dashboards already exist, all with ad-hoc SQL. Where do you start?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Not by trying to model every metric in the business before anyone gets to use the layer — that's a multi-quarter project with no visible win along the way, and it's easy for leadership to lose patience with. I'd start by finding the metrics that are already actively disputed — usually revenue and some active-user variant — because those are the cases where inconsistency is already visible and painful, so proving the fix there gets buy-in fast.

Concretely: pick the two or three highest-traffic, most argued-about metrics, define them properly in the layer with an explicit owner, migrate the handful of dashboards that matter most onto them, and show the reconciliation — "these two reports now agree, and here's the definition everyone can inspect." That's the case study that gets the next twenty teams to ask to be migrated rather than having migration forced on them.

The forty-dashboard backlog then becomes an ongoing, lower-priority migration rather than a blocking prerequisite — new dashboards get built through the layer by default going forward, and old ones migrate opportunistically whenever they're touched for other reasons. I'd explicitly avoid treating "100% migrated" as the finish line; partial coverage on the highest-value metrics delivers most of the value early.

**Testing:** whether you can sequence an organizational rollout by leverage and visible wins instead of attempting full coverage up front.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Rollout strategy

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between "headless BI" and a normal BI tool setup, and why would an organization care?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
In a normal setup, metric definitions live inside a specific BI tool's own configuration — a calculated field in Looker, a custom field in Tableau — siloed to that tool. If two teams use different BI tools, their metric definitions are two independent things that happen to have the same name, with no guarantee they compute the same value.

"Headless BI" flips that: the metrics layer is the source of truth, defined independently of any visualization tool, and every BI tool is just a front end that queries the layer by metric name. The tool becomes replaceable — swap Looker for a different tool tomorrow and the metric definitions carry over unchanged, because they never lived inside Looker to begin with.

The organizational reason to care is real switching cost and consistency risk. I've seen a company avoid a genuinely painful BI-tool migration specifically because their metrics were headless — the new tool just pointed at the existing layer, instead of a team spending weeks re-implementing forty calculated fields and hoping they matched the old tool's results exactly.

**Testing:** whether you understand headless BI as a decoupling strategy, not just a buzzword for "metrics layer."
